propositions.text: I dismiss this appeal.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal.

propositions.text: The Appellant is a citizen of India claiming refugee protection due to fear of persecution based on imputed political opinion and being a westernized woman.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of India. The Appellant claims refugee protection because she fears persecution India on the basis of imputed political opinion, and because she is a woman who is "westernized."

propositions.text: The RPD found the Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Bengaluru, India.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the Appellant has an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in India in the city of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore.)

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, noting the Appellant is an Indian citizen fearing persecution for imputed political opinion and westernization; the RPD found an IFA in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: The RPD erred in finding the Appellant has an IFA because agents of persecution would locate her there due to her online presence and activism.
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding she has an IFA because the agents of persecution would locate her in the IFA due to her online presence and that her activism would put her at particular risk in Bengaluru.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in finding an IFA because persecution agents would find her in Bengaluru due to her online activism.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is whether the RPD erred in finding the Appellant has a viable IFA.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is whether the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant has a viable IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the key issue as whether the RPD erred in finding a viable IFA for the Appellant.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err and the Appellant has an IFA in Bengaluru.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err. I find that the Appellant has an IFA in Bengaluru.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD did not err and that the Appellant has an IFA in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal; the RPD was correct that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention2 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agreeing the RPD correctly found the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.

propositions.text: The Appellant came to Canada in 2013 on a student visa and did not complete her studies.
propositions.quote: The Appellant came to Canada from India in 2013 on a student visa. The Appellant testified at the RPD hearing that she had difficulty pursuing her studies and did not receive a diploma or certificate.

propositions.text: The Minister provided evidence that the Appellant was arrested by CBSA in 2019 for suspected misrepresentation and non-compliance with study permit conditions.
propositions.quote: The Minister provided evidence that the Appellant was arrested by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) on January 30, 2019 on suspicion that she misrepresented information on a work permit application and that she was not compliant with the conditions of her study permit.

propositions.text: The Appellant filed a refugee claim while in CBSA custody and testified she was unaware she could file before arrest.
propositions.quote: The Appellant filed a claim for refugee protection while in CBSA custody. The Appellant testified at the RPD hearing that she had not filed a claim for refugee protection in Canada before she was arrested because she was unaware that she could do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts the Appellant's arrival in Canada, study difficulties, arrest by CBSA, and refugee claim filed in custody.

propositions.text: In her BOC, the Appellant fears persecution in India based on imputed political opinion and as a westernized woman social group member.
propositions.quote: In her Basis of Claim (BOC) form, the Appellant submits that she fears persecution in India based on: a. imputed political opinion given because her father is active in the political Bharatiya Janata Party, and, b. membership in a particular social group because she would be persecuted as a "westernized" woman

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant's BOC states fear of persecution due to imputed political opinion and being a westernized woman social group member.

propositions.text: The Appellant has posted support for women's issues online for about five years, increasing activity before the RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: The Appellant says that she has been posting her support of women's issues in India online from Canada for approximately five years before the RPD hearing. She became more active online within the two months before the date of the RPD hearing, creating an Instagram account where has about 40 follows, and a blog that she has linked to her personal Facebook account which has about 100 followers.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant has supported women's issues online for five years, increasing activity shortly before the RPD hearing.

propositions.text: The RAD requested a submission on item 12.8 in the India NDP dated July 17, 2020, which is accepted into the record.
propositions.quote: At the request of the RAD, the Appellant made a submission regarding item 12.8 in the National Documentation Package (NDP) for India dated July 17, 2020. I accept the submission into the record and I will refer to this submission in my analysis.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to introduce late new evidence to the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also seeks to introduce late new evidence to the RAD.

propositions.text: The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected.
propositions.quote: The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected

paragraphs.summary: The RAD requested and accepted a submission on item 12.8 in the India NDP; the Appellant seeks to introduce late evidence, which is rejected.

propositions.text: The Appellant seeks to introduce seven online media articles as late new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellant seeks to introduce the following as late new evidence: 1. Online Media Article: It's a Myth, women in Bengaluru don't feel safe either (December 3, 2019); 2. CTV News Online Media Article: Indian police accused of forcing cremation of gang rape victim (September 30, 2020); 3. Online Media Article: How women in India faced brutal sexual assault over time (October 4, 2020); 4. Online Media Article: NCRB data: At 47, highest rape with murder incidents reported from Maharashtra (October 2,2020); 5. Online Media Article: New App helps keep track of those under home quarantine. (April 10, 2020); 6. Online Media Article: Police to keep track of home-quarantined. (December 10, 2020); and, 7. Online Media Article: Government publishes details of 19,240 home-quarantined people to keep a check. (May 25, 2020)

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant seeks to introduce seven online media articles as late new evidence.

propositions.text: Evidence can be accepted only if it arose after the RPD decision, was not reasonably available before, or could not reasonably have been brought earlier.
propositions.quote: According to the law, I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or, iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

paragraphs.summary: The law permits accepting evidence only if it arose after the RPD decision, was unavailable before, or could not reasonably have been brought earlier.

propositions.text: If evidence meets requirements, it must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: Evidence meeting timing requirements must also be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.

propositions.text: The content of evidence, not date, is determinative for admissibility after claim rejection; burden is on Appellant.
propositions.quote: In terms of evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim, it is the content of the evidence and not the date of the document that is determinative. With respect to the admissibility of new evidence, the burden lies with the Appellant.

propositions.text: RAD applies a narrow interpretation of section 110(4); not an opportunity to complete a deficient record.
propositions.quote: The RAD applies a narrow interpretation of section 110(4). This is not an opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD.

propositions.text: Full and detailed submissions on admissibility and relevancy of new evidence are expected.
propositions.quote: It is expected that full and detailed submissions on the admissibility and the relevancy of the proposed new evidence will be included.

paragraphs.summary: The court states content, not date, determines admissibility; burden is on Appellant; RAD narrowly interprets section 110(4); full submissions expected.

propositions.text: In deciding late evidence admissibility, consider relevance, new evidence, and whether it could have been provided earlier with reasonable effort.
propositions.quote: In deciding whether to allow an application for late submissions or late evidence, I must consider any relevant factors, including: a) the document's relevance and probative value; b) any new evidence the document brings to the appeal; and, c) whether the person who is the subject of the appeal, with reasonable effort, could have provided the document or written submissions with the Appellant's record, respondent's record or reply record.

paragraphs.summary: The court must consider relevance, newness, and whether the evidence could have been provided earlier when deciding on late evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant argues the documents are highly relevant and probative to the IFA issue and could not have been provided earlier.
propositions.quote: Further, the Claimant makes an application to submit documents and written submissions that were not previously provided in accordance with Rule 37 of the RAD rules. The documentary evidence is further provided by way of affidavit. This document is highly relevant and probative to the determinative issue of IFA, and could not have been provided with the Appellant's record.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the documents are highly relevant to IFA and could not have been provided earlier.

propositions.text: The Appellant did not submit full and detailed submissions on admissibility and relevance as expected.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has not submitted full and detailed submissions on the admissibility and relevance of the proposed new evidence as expected.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant failed to submit full and detailed submissions on admissibility and relevance of new evidence.

propositions.text: The Appellant failed to establish admissibility of the proposed new evidence.
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has failed to establish the admissibility of the documents she seeks to introduce as new evidence for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appellant failed to establish admissibility of the new evidence.

propositions.text: Item 1 article predates appeal perfection; no explanation for late submission or source credibility provided; article is interviews and statements.
propositions.quote: Item 1, an online media article titled It's a Myth, women in Bengaluru don't feel safe either is dated December 3, 2019 which pre-dates the perfection of the Appellant's appeal on February 18, 2020. The Appellant has not provided an explanation why the document was not submitted at perfection. The Appellant has not provided information regarding the source and credibility of this document. The article is a collection of short interviews and statements.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Item 1 article predates appeal perfection, lacks explanation for late submission and source credibility.

propositions.text: Item 2 article postdates RPD decision and appeal perfection; CTV is credible; article lacks Bengaluru reference; relevance not explained.
propositions.quote: Item 2 is a CTV News Online Media Article: Indian police accused of forcing cremation of gang rape victim is dated September 30, 2020 and therefore arises after the RPD decision and after the perfection of the Appellant's appeal. CTV is a credible Canadian news organization. The article does not contain any reference to Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Item 2 article postdates RPD decision, is from credible source, but lacks Bengaluru reference and relevance explanation.

propositions.text: Item 3 article postdates appeal perfection; no credibility explanation; lacks Bengaluru info; relevance not explained.
propositions.quote: Item 3 is an online media article dated October 4, 2020 titled, How women in India faced brutal sexual assault over time. The article arose after the perfection of the Appellant's appeal. The Appellant has not provided any explanation as to the credibility of the online source. The article does not contain any information about Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Item 3 article postdates appeal perfection, lacks credibility explanation, Bengaluru info, and relevance explanation.

propositions.text: Appellant did not explain source or credibility of online article item 4, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to determinative issue
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not provided any explanation as to the source and credibility of this online article. The article does not contain any information about Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant did not explain the source or credibility of item 4, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to the determinative issue.

propositions.text: Appellant did not explain credibility of online article item 5, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to determinative issue
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not provided any explanation as to the credibility of the online source. The article does not contain any information about Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant did not explain credibility of item 5, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to the determinative issue.

propositions.text: Appellant did not explain credibility of online article item 6, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to determinative issue
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not provided any explanation as to the credibility of the online source. The article does not contain any information about Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant did not explain credibility of item 6, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to the determinative issue.

propositions.text: Appellant did not explain credibility of online article item 7, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to determinative issue
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not provided any explanation as to the credibility of the online source. The article does not contain any information about Bengaluru. The Appellant has not set out what new evidence this article provides with respect to the determinative issue and how this article is relevant to the determinative issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant did not explain credibility of item 7, which lacks Bengaluru info and relevance to the determinative issue.

propositions.text: No new evidence admitted, so no grounds to allow appellant's hearing request
propositions.quote: Given that I have not admitted new evidence, I have no grounds to allow the Appellant's request for a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes no new evidence was admitted, so it denies the appellant's request for a hearing.

propositions.text: Role is to assess all evidence and decide if RPD decision was correct
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

propositions.text: Conducted independent assessment of evidence and arguments
propositions.quote: As part of my analysis, I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence and the arguments.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role is to assess all evidence and decide if the RPD decision was correct, having conducted an independent assessment.

propositions.text: Presumption that sworn allegations before IRB are true unless reason to doubt; does not apply to inferences or speculation without evidence
propositions.quote: When a person swears to the truth of certain allegations before the Immigration and Refugee Board, there is a presumption that those allegations are true unless there is a reason to doubt their truthfulness. This presumption of truthfulness does not apply to inferences or conclusions a witness may draw from facts, or to speculation for which there is no evidentiary basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the presumption that sworn allegations before IRB are true unless doubted, but not for inferences or speculation without evidence.

propositions.text: Presumption of truth may be rebutted by contradictions, inconsistencies, omissions, vague testimony, limited knowledge, or false documents
propositions.quote: The presumption that a person's sworn testimony is true may be rebutted where problems are identified with the testimony. These problems can include contradictions, inconsistencies, and omissions; incoherent or vague testimony; limited knowledge of key elements of the case; or a reliance on false documents.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the presumption of truth can be rebutted by contradictions, inconsistencies, omissions, vague testimony, limited knowledge, or false documents.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding appellant has an IFA in Bengaluru, India
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that he has an IFA in India in Bengaluru.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred in finding he has an IFA in Bengaluru, India.

propositions.text: IFA test requires balance of probabilities no serious persecution risk in IFA and reasonableness of seeking refuge there
propositions.quote: The adjudicating panel must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that: (1) there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted or, on the balance of probabilities, subjected to a risk to life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the IFA and; (2) that conditions in that part of the country are such that it would be reasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the IFA test requires balance of probabilities no serious persecution risk and reasonableness of seeking refuge there.

propositions.text: Claimant must establish inexistence of IFA by showing risk throughout country and unreasonableness of IFA
propositions.quote: Jurisprudence sets out that "it is up to the refugee claimant to establish the inexistence of an IFA according to the two-part test: applicants must establish that they are at risk throughout their country and that the IFA would be objectively unreasonable given the circumstances."

paragraphs.summary: Jurisprudence requires claimants to prove no IFA by showing risk throughout country and IFA unreasonableness.

propositions.text: Appellant must prove serious persecution risk in IFA; RPD found appellant failed burden; court finds no error
propositions.quote: The onus is on the Appellant to adduce sufficient credible evidence that she faces a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFAs. The Appellant must establish that the agents of persecution have the means and motivation to harm her in the IFA. The RPD found that the Appellant has not met this burden of proof. I find that the RPD did not err for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant failed to prove serious persecution risk in IFA and the RPD did not err in this finding.

propositions.text: Appellant's family returned to village, faces verbal harassment but no harm since 2018
propositions.quote: The Appellant testified at the RPD hearing that her family has returned to their village and continues to live there. The Appellant testified that her family continues to be verbally harassed and threatened in the village by her father's political adversaries; however, family members have not been harmed since their return to the village in the summer of 2018 at the invitation of the local mayor.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found appellant's family returned to village, faces verbal harassment but no harm since 2018.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding appellant's belief of being located via online postings is speculative
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the Appellant's belief that she will be located through her online postings is speculative.

propositions.text: No evidence that political adversaries try to locate appellant to harm her in IFA; RPD did not err
propositions.quote: I find the RPD did not err. I have no evidence before me that her father's political adversaries are attempting to locate the Appellant in order to harm her or that they would attempt to locate the Appellant in the IFA location in order to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues RPD erred on speculation about being located online; court finds no evidence and no error by RPD.

propositions.text: RPD erred in finding IFA reasonable, failed to apply evidence on online activism correctly
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred in finding that the IFA would be reasonable; "The Appellant further submits that the Member failed to correctly apply the evidence proffered with respect to the Appellant's online activism and activity, and make the correct inferences from same with respect to the reasonableness of the IFA."

propositions.text: RPD did not err in finding IFA reasonable for reasons that follow
propositions.quote: I find the RPD did not err for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues RPD erred on IFA reasonableness and online activism evidence; court finds no error.

propositions.text: RPD noted Bengaluru is 2,500 km from Punjab; main languages Hindi and English, which appellant speaks
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that Bengaluru is approximately 2,500 kilometres from the state of Punjab. The RPD cited documentary evidence that the main languages in Bengaluru are Hindi and English. The Appellant testifies that she speaks both Hindi and English in addition to her native Punjabi.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD noted Bengaluru's distance from Punjab and languages, which appellant speaks.

propositions.text: RPD cited evidence Bengaluru is preferred city for single women migrating for work and study
propositions.quote: The RPD cited objective documentary evidence in the NDP that Bengaluru is the most preferred city for single women in India who have migrated for employment and study.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD cited evidence Bengaluru is preferred city for single women migrating for employment and study.

propositions.text: RPD cited evidence of high discrimination and violence against women in India but not rising to persecution
propositions.quote: The RPD cited objective documentary evidence that there are high levels of discrimination and violence against women in India, but that the general level of societal discrimination against women in India does not rise to the level of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD cited evidence of high discrimination and violence against women in India but not persecution level.

propositions.text: RPD noted small Sikh community in Bengaluru; Sikhs generally safe but face localized discrimination
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that there is a small Sikh community in Bengaluru. Objective documentary evidence in the NPD establishes that there have been instances where Sikhs have been subjected to discrimination in Indian society and to harsh treatment within the Indian judicial system. Nonetheless the evidence states that: According to Australia's DFAT report, "since the late 1980s and early 1990s, Sikhs have lived peacefully in India and the majority of Sikhs do not experience societal discrimination or violence" (Australia 17 Oct. 2018, para. 3.19). In a telephone interview with the Research Directorate, an associate professor at Hiram College researching South Asian politics similarly stated that Sikhs outside Punjab are economically and socially integrated in the communities in which they live and are generally safe, although there is localized discrimination, such as the forced baptism of Sikhs, blocking of entry to public areas without removing articles of faith, such as being asked to remove turbans or kirpans for entrance tests to educational programs, but that these matters are usually dealt with by local courts or police (Associate Professor 26 Sept. 2019). According to the joint response by the WSO representative and the Associate Professor, Sikhs may encounter difficulties integrating in areas where a Sikh community does not exist and, especially for practicing Sikhs, "in other Indian states that are not as familiar with the Sikh identity" (WSO and Associate Professor 3 May 2019).

paragraphs.summary: The RPD noted a small Sikh community in Bengaluru; Sikhs generally safe but face localized discrimination.

propositions.text: IFA unreasonable due to appellant's online activism making her a target in India
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the IFA is unreasonable because the Appellant's online activism would make her a target in India.

propositions.text: Appellant did not provide credible evidence of risk in Bengaluru from online activities; no credible threats shown
propositions.quote: The Appellant has not adduced sufficient credible evidence to establish that she would be at risk in Bengaluru due to her online activities and that Bengaluru would therefore be unreasonable as an IFA. The Appellant has submitted evidence that she received an anonymous online threat in response to her online activity in Canada. I have no evidence before me that she has received credible threats that would put her at risk in Bengaluru.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues IFA unreasonable due to online activism risk; court finds no credible evidence or threats in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: The Federal Court of Appeal sets a very high threshold for the second prong of the IFA test requiring conditions jeopardizing life or safety
propositions.quote: the Federal Court of Appeal has set a very high threshold with respect to the second prong: ...In Ranganathan, after citing long passages from Justice Linden's reasons in Thirunavukkarasu v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1994] 1 FC 589, and emphasizing the parts where the Court of Appeal insists that the IFA's attractiveness is irrelevant, the Court of Appeal found as follows: [15] We read the decision of Linden J.A. for this Court as setting up a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. It requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant in travelling or temporarily relocating to a safe area.

propositions.text: Actual and concrete evidence of jeopardizing conditions is required for the second prong of the IFA test
propositions.quote: In addition, it requires actual and concrete evidence of such conditions.

propositions.text: Absence of relatives in a safe place only amounts to jeopardizing conditions if it threatens life or safety
propositions.quote: The absence of relatives in a safe place, whether taken alone or in conjunction with other factors, can only amount to such condition if it meets that threshold, that is to say if it establishes that, as a result, a claimant's life or safety would be jeopardized.

propositions.text: Loss of employment, status, quality of life, aspirations, or frustration of wishes does not meet the high threshold for IFA unreasonableness
propositions.quote: This is in sharp contrast with undue hardship resulting from loss of employment, loss of status, reduction in quality of life, loss of aspirations, loss of beloved ones and frustration of one's wishes and expectations.

propositions.text: Distinction between refugee claims and humanitarian and compassionate applications should not be blurred
propositions.quote: As noted by the Court at paragraph 17, the distinction between refugee claims and humanitarian and compassionate applications should not be blurred.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court of Appeal requires actual, concrete jeopardizing conditions for IFA unreasonableness, not hardships or absence of relatives, per prior cases.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not shown conditions jeopardizing her life or safety in the proposed IFAs
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has not provided evidence of conditions that would jeopardize her life and safety in the proposed IFAs.

propositions.text: Challenges in relocating to Bengaluru are significant but insufficient to meet the stringent second prong of the IFA test
propositions.quote: While the Appellant would undoubtedly face significant challenges in relocating to Bengaluru, I find that these challenges are not sufficient to satisfy the stringent requirements set out in the second prong of the IFA test in order for an IFA to be considered unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant's challenges relocating to Bengaluru do not meet the high threshold for IFA unreasonableness.

propositions.text: The Appellant has a viable IFA in Bengaluru
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has a viable IFA in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: The Appellant does not have a Section 97 claim
propositions.quote: The Appellant does not have a Section 97 claim

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant has a viable IFA in Bengaluru and no Section 97 claim.

propositions.text: The RPD erred by not analyzing the Appellant's claim under section 97 of IRPA
propositions.quote: The Appellant argues on appeal that the RPD erred by not conducting an analysis of the Appellant's claim under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err in its handling of the section 97 claim
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues RPD erred by not analyzing section 97 claim; the court finds no error by RPD.

propositions.text: The RPD's test for a viable IFA under section 97 requires balance of probabilities that claimant faces personal danger of torture or cruel and unusual punishment
propositions.quote: In its decision, the RPD set out the test for a viable IFA under section 97. "I must be satisfied that one; on a balance of probabilities the claimant would not be subject personally to a danger of torture or to a risk of life or cruel and unusual punishment..."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD's section 97 test requires personal risk of torture or cruel punishment on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Appellant's Counsel argued Appellant has a section 97 claim due to personal risk as an educated, artistic woman active online supporting women's issues
propositions.quote: In his submissions to the RPD, Appellant's Counsel argued that the Appellant has a section 97 claim because she is an educated, artistic woman who is active online in support of women's issues and who would therefore be at risk in India.

propositions.text: To succeed under section 97, claimant must show personal risk not shared generally in society
propositions.quote: In order to succeed as a section 97 claim, jurisprudence requires that the Appellant must establish that she faces a personal risk to her life or a personal risk of cruel and unusual punishment, and that this risk must not be a general risk that is shared with others in society.

propositions.text: The risk claimed by the Appellant is a general risk shared with other educated, artistic women supporting women's issues online in India
propositions.quote: I find that the risk the Appellant claims she faces is a general risk that she shares with other educated, artistic women in India who support women's issues online.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant claims section 97 risk as an educated, artistic woman online; court finds risk is general, not personal.

propositions.text: The Appellant has not established a section 97 risk in Bengaluru, the identified IFA
propositions.quote: I find that the Appellant has not established that she faces a section 97 risk in India in Bengaluru, the identified IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellant has not established a section 97 risk in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision confirmed that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is a neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee or protection status.
